messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Rivas had been proud of how self-possessed she was at fifty-three, a seasoned stock broker in Miami who could manage volatile markets, difficult clients, and the pressure of being the person others looked to when numbers turned ugly. The mugging happened one winter evening after she left her office later than usual, crossing a nearly empty parking garage with her laptop bag tucked close under her arm. Two men appeared from between the concrete pillars. One moved abruptly toward her while the other angled behind her, and the suddenness of it—the quick step, the sharp reach for her bag, the feeling that she had been cornered before she could even think—lodged in her body as horror and fear. For months after, ordinary movements from strangers could send her instantly on guard, and even the clatter of a dropped tray in a café or a car backfiring in the street made her jump in a way that embarrassed her. She found herself constantly scanning doorways, mirrors, and parked cars, taking in exits and faces before she was aware she was doing it, as though vigilance might keep her one step ahead of danger.

What disturbed Marisol most was not only the robbery itself but how little she believed anyone had truly protected her. Security had been “around,” the garage had cameras, and yet in the moment she felt abandoned by the very systems that were supposed to make a professional building safe. She became convinced that the world was a dangerous place in a way she had once considered exaggerated or naive. At the same time, she felt emotionally hollow, as if some essential part of her had gone dead inside. That deadness sat beside a wash of fear, anger, shame, and guilt she could not organize or set aside. Because she believed danger could appear anywhere and that institutions had failed her when it mattered, she began to move through her days with a careful, appeasing politeness she had not needed before. She overexplained herself to doormen, smiled too quickly at men who came too close in elevators, and became unnaturally compliant when she felt threatened, handing over her purse or stepping aside before anyone had even asked. She told herself that if she was agreeable enough, attentive enough, and quiet enough, she might prevent a repeat of that night.

The fear did not stay abstract. A sudden movement by a stranger in the subway station near her office, a hand darting into a coat pocket, or even a colleague standing up too fast in a meeting could make her heart pound and her shoulders lock. Those moments fed the same grim conclusion: she lived in a world where danger could break through at any time. In response, Marisol doubled down on habits that she believed would keep catastrophe away. She performed mental rituals before leaving home—counting, repeating phrases under her breath, mentally checking that she had “covered” each possible risk—because she was certain that if she did not keep her mind orderly, something bad would happen again. The rituals offered brief relief, but they also reinforced the sense that danger was everywhere and that she had to work constantly to stay ahead of it. Each time she tried to manage her fear that way, the world seemed more perilous, and her thoughts returned to the same bleak appraisal: if the people and institutions around her had failed once, they could fail again.

Over the following months, the pattern narrowed her life. At work, in the glass-walled brokerage office where colleagues moved quickly behind her chair and clients arrived unpredictably, Marisol found herself monitoring every sound and movement instead of following market data with her usual focus. She avoided staying late, took longer routes to the parking structure, and began asking her husband to pick her up whenever possible. Her husband noticed that she flinched when he came up behind her in the kitchen and that she had grown quieter at home, as if the emotional numbness made conversation effortful. She was ashamed of how dependent and accommodating she had become, yet the more threatened she felt, the more she fell back into compliance and scanning, and the more certain she became that vigilance was the only thing standing between her and another attack. That certainty, in turn, deepened her belief that the world could not be trusted and that she had been left to fend for herself.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was exhausted by living as though every corner might hide the same threat. She came in after a week in which a sudden shout in the office lobby left her shaking for an hour, and after realizing she had spent more time rehearsing safety in her head than sleeping. What brought her to treatment was the fear that this way of living was shrinking her marriage, her work, and the confident life she had built. She was most afraid that if she did not find a way to feel safe again, she would remain deadened inside and forever braced for the next sudden movement in a world she no longer trusted.
